chapter_theme: Manimidaipavalam 161-180: separation for wealth and war argued from both sides of the road, the friend's dissuasions and comforts, the marutham quarrel heard from wife and other woman, and the press toward marriage in the hills.

161.reading: The friend asks the man what this leaving for work can mean: has the girl already heard that he means to cross, for wealth, the frightening forest where hard-eyed archers kill travellers and the red-eared vulture calls its kin to the carrion, since her many-petalled eyes are already pouring tears onto her young breasts?
161.nuance: The friend never reports the departure to the girl; she argues that the girl has read it in him before any word was spoken, so her tears are the friend's whole case for stopping him. The forest is given as the man's own reported resolve (பொருள் புரிந்து இறப்ப எண்ணினர்), set inside quotation, as if overheard.

thinai_evidence.note: a man resolved to cross the waste for wealth

comparisons.tenor: her young breasts, risen as if a tormenting power

colophon.thurai: பிரிவுணர்த்தியதோழி, தலைமகளதுவேறுபாடு கண்டு முன்னமேஉணர்ந்தாள் நம்பெருமாட்டியென்று தலைமகனைச்செலவு விலக்கியது.

162.reading: Leaving after a night meeting, the man tells his heart how, at midnight in a storm whose lightning split a sky like the sea, he stood by one corner of her father's guarded house until the guards slackened, and she came, trembling like a shoot in the wind, and held him till his sickness eased: she who is as hard to win as the goddesses of the high slope where waterfalls shine like the Pandiyan's flag, on the hill of Athigan who never fails a suppliant.
162.nuance: The danger he braved (the storm, the guards, the father's house) is the proof of love he offers his own heart, and the closing image places her among the hill goddesses, beyond reach even while just embraced. Lines 1 and 2 are obscure: they seem to describe the unmeasurable dark mass of cloud drawn from the deep, but the word division is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: a secret night meeting at her father's house in the hills

comparisons.tenor: the wide sky, like the sea
lightning, like a creeper of flame
her hair, gleaming like rippled dark sand
her rain-cool eyes, like flowers in her bright face
her white teeth, like a row of buds
her trembling, like a tender shoot in the wind
the shining waterfalls, like the Pandiyan's victorious flag on his elephants
the girl, as hard to win as the goddesses of the slope

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிக்கண்தலைமகளைக் கண்ணுற்று நீங்கிய தலைமகன் தன்நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

163.reading: Alone at the end of the rains, bangles slipping as she thinks of the man who went, the woman turns on the cold north wind of the early-dew midnight, whose spray like an elephant's breath scorches the lotus: it seems to have come for her alone, so let it go, as unrelenting as she is, to the land where the cruel one went; those eager in their work may yet remember.
163.nuance: She sends her tormentor as her messenger: the wind that melts her heart like a heap of fine sand in a stream is told to do the same to him. The last line is a hope that slips out under the anger: men intent on work also remember.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits at home at the turn of the season, watching for his return

comparisons.tenor: the wind's spray, like an elephant's breath
the cold of the north wind, as if a hill had melted
her heart dissolving like a heap of fine sand laid by a stream

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem itself addresses the north wind

164.reading: In the war camp the man tells his heart that the rains have restored the sun-cracked land, bees hum over mullai and glory lilies and the forest is fragrant: this is the season when she who lives in pain, eyes dripping, wondering how he fares, would regain her old beauty, if only the fierce king would release them from the work of his fort-breaking elephants.
164.nuance: The season he promised has come and he is held by another's war: the elephant that smashes forts and snaps its tethering post is the king's power, and also an image of the restraint he himself cannot break.

thinai_evidence.note: mullai flowers in the first heavy rains

comparisons.tenor: the sun's rays as hands that draw up the land's yield

165.reading: Onlookers describe the house after the daughter has gone off across many lands with her lover: her playmates have put off their ornaments and mourn, and the mother, crying 'give me your sweet shoulder, let my life end', strokes eyes and brow, rests in the striped shade of the nochi the girl used to touch, crowns her doll with fading kuvalai from the water-pot and embraces it weeping, 'this doll lying in the sand is my precious daughter'.
165.nuance: Lines 1 to 5 describe the lands the girl crossed: an elephant calf, frightened by the male's trumpeting when its mother fell into a pit, drinking from a buffalo's udder in an old town. Read as a hidden sense (the young parted from its mother and fed at another's breast) it would mirror the daughter, but the syntax of line 3 (எந்த) is unclear, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has left with her lover across many lands

comparisons.tenor: the doll taken for the daughter herself

166.reading: The other woman mocks the husband who soothes his wife with an oath ('may the fearsome god at the gate of Velur strike me if I was ever at that woman's shoulder'): if that is he, then who was it, friend, that yesterday clasped the head-float with us and, decked as for a wedding, bathed in the Kaveri's new flood?
166.nuance: She speaks so that the wife's people will hear, turning the god he swore by against him; the oath is set at Velur, where broken toddy jars chill the street like rain, so the shrine's grandeur makes the perjury worse.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's affair and his false oath to his wife

comparisons.tenor: the street chilled by spilt toddy as by drizzling rain

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: the parathai addresses her own friend so that the wife's people overhear

colophon.thurai: பரத்தையொடு புனல்ஆடிய தலைமகன் தலைமகளிடைப் புக்கு யான்-ஆடிற்றிலன் என்று சூளுற்றான் என்பது கேட்ட 3பரத்தைதன் பாங்காயினார் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது.

167.reading: Pressed by his heart to go for wealth, the man asks it: after tonight, spent sweetly with his dark-skinned wife in a sky-touching mansion, shall they tomorrow lie sleepless in the ruined public hall of a village the people fled for fear of caravan-raiding archers, where an elephant rubbing its back has toppled the brick wall, the doves have left, the painted god has gone and the unswept floor forgets its offerings, and termites roof the rafters? So he gives up the journey.
167.nuance: The ruin is built point by point against the bedroom: gems against termites, a made bed against a cracked floor, a full house against one even its god has deserted. The desolation of the road is what keeps him home, not her plea.

thinai_evidence.note: the deserted village of the robber-haunted waste

168.reading: The friend tells the hill-man that, having spent the night watch with him, they are left love-sick with wet eyes, and he must stop: will he still come at night, when the hunters sleep, down the narrow deer-path of the great slope where waterfalls roar like the kitchen of Udhiyan at Kuzhumur, where a male elephant, embracing the female who has just calved, guards the sleep of their swaying calf, and a fierce striped tiger roars in its cave?
168.nuance: The path is drawn to frighten (the tiger, the dark) and to instruct (the elephant family): the danger argues against night visits, the guarded calf argues for a household.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend ends the lovers' night meetings in the hills

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the waterfalls, like the din of Udhiyan's kitchen

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon has தலைமகளை, but the poem addresses the hero (வெற்ப)

iraicchi.act: the male elephant embraces the female who has just calved and guards their calf's sleep
iraicchi.sense: the man who crosses this slope sees what he should be: a mate keeping a household, not a night visitor

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்ததலைமகளை இரவுக்குறி விலக்கி வரைவு கடாயது.

169.reading: Halfway across the waste the man tells his heart how she must be suffering: on a burnt clearing where hunters roast on a fire-drill blaze the elephant meat a tiger left and salt-carriers cook rice with spring water and the sea's nectar, he has crossed many such wastes, while she, pale and thinking long in the lonely dimming evening, fingers to her brow, tears running, shoulders wasted, grieves.
169.nuance: Both halves are pictures of evening: the travellers' camp fire on the road and her vigil at home, so the man sees his own night and hers at once. The tears 'like water a kayal fish spits' turn her fish-shaped eyes into the simile's source.

thinai_evidence.note: the scorched waste he has crossed

comparisons.tenor: salt, as the nectar the sea grows
her tears, like water a kayal fish spits

170.reading: With no one else to carry her word (the grove, the backwater and the punnai will not speak), the woman begs the crab to tell the lord of the shore, where bees drunk on neythal scent falter in flight, that at midnight, while the small sea-crow wearied on the thazhai bough dreams of prawns beside its mate, she asks whether the one who cured his pain must now swim through her own.
170.nuance: Her message turns on a reversal: she once relieved his distress, and he leaves her to drown in hers. The bees that sip and then falter echo the lord of the shore himself.

thinai_evidence.note: punnai, neythal and the shore lord of the backwaters

comparisons.tenor: the neythal blooms of the backwater, like eyes
the bees take the neythal's scent as nectar

iraicchi.act: the small sea-crow rests through midnight beside its mate on the thazhai bough
iraicchi.sense: even the weary crow sleeps paired while she lies awake alone, which is the wrong he has done her

171.reading: The friend tells the woman not to grieve endlessly that her brow pales, her shoulders lose their bamboo-like beauty and she thinks of him daily: he will come back to her, the man who, set on wealth, crossed the waste where, because hill villagers roam with bows to hear the tiger's call, the bear leaves the honey below and climbs the black iruppai to eat its sweet flowers like fruit.
171.nuance: The bear that changes its food for fear of the hunters is only the road, but it shows a creature adapting to danger, which is what the friend asks of her.

thinai_evidence.note: he crossed the waste for wealth and she must bear it

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders, with the beauty of chosen bamboo
the iruppai's pulpy flowers, like fruit

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளைத் தோழி வற்புறீஇயது.

172.reading: The friend tells the hill-man that on his slopes, where a honeyed waterfall sounds like drums, the iron-armed hunter kills an elephant, plants its tusk at his grass hut and feasts with his kin on jackfruit liquor and meat roasted on sandal brands; she never knew he was loveless, and had she known, gold-coloured pallor would not have spread over the girl's gem-like beauty.
172.nuance: The hunter's catalogue is of a man who takes, keeps and celebrates with his kin; the friend's reproach is that the hill-man has done only the taking. The reproach is aimed at marriage, as the colophon says.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill hunter and his slopes

comparisons.tenor: the waterfall's sound, like resounding drums
the hunter's black arm, like wrought iron
the jackfruit, like a drum
her beauty, like a gem
pallor, the colour of gold

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகளை இடத்துஉய்த்துவந்து தலைமகனை வரைவு கடாயது.

173.reading: The friend tells the woman he will come: set on his work, he said that never straying from dharma and propping up kin in their misfortunes are not for those who sit at ease, asked her to bear the hard sorrow a few days and straightened her bangles; then he crossed the gold-bearing slopes of Nannan's sky-touching range, where deer flee the salt-carriers' shouts and drought-split bamboo throws out pearls like kazhangu seeds.
173.nuance: The comfort is built on the man's own maxim: wealth is what makes dharma and help to kin possible, so his going is a duty, and the gesture of straightening her bangles seals the promise.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone across the hills for work

comparisons.tenor: the bamboo pearls, shining like kazhangu seeds

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளைத் தோழி வற்புறுத்தியது.

174.reading: In the war camp, having declared that victory now rests with the side that can turn back the attacking army with one force and set aside the drum that calls men to take the battle-flower, the man tells his heart she does not know he is coming: as the mullai sprouts under the morning rain, at every thunder she must shrink, helpless and resentful, pale with sorrow, she with spots on her breast like ripe vengai flowers and soft few steps on the sand.
174.nuance: The reading of lines 1 to 5 is uncertain: they may mean that he has declined the call to further battle and is going home, or that he went to war without her knowing. Either way the poem's present is her not knowing, while the rain she reads as betrayal is the season of his return.

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai creeper under the rain clouds

comparisons.tenor: the spots on her breast, like ripe vengai flowers

175.reading: The woman reminds her friend that the man who crossed the hot waste, where archers' whistling arrows take travellers' lives and vultures call their flock to the carrion, swore hard vows, held her bangled wrist and said he would come back with the work done when the cool clouds came down, flashing more often than the spear Chezhiyan raised after winning at Alangaanam, thundering like drums, the rainbow arched like the garland on the wheel-bearing god's chest, and the earth's yield flowering: and that time is now.
175.nuance: The poem calls the lover's promise a வஞ்சினம், the word for a warrior's vow, and frames the season of its testing with a king's victory and a god's garland, so a private promise is measured against the public oaths of puram. Against the friend's comfort she sets the season itself as evidence.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits for the return promised for the rains, which have come

comparisons.tenor: the lightning, flashing more often than Chezhiyan's raised spear
the thunder, like war drums
the rainbow, like the garland on the wheel-bearing god's chest

colophon.thurai: பிரிவின்கண்வற்புறுக்குந் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச்சொற்றதூ உமாம்.

176.reading: The friend refuses the husband at the door: lord of a town where, in a lotus pond wide as the sea, a long-eyed water crab, afraid of the white heron hunting for food, runs across the mud and hides in its water-filled hole, has your new beloved turned angry because you let go her bangled hand in the festival dance, so you come here? what does she owe, she who has borne no son and does not keep your house as we do? she weeps her painted face away, snaps her fingers red and blunts her teeth: go, so that she who tells the whole town about you may see you.
176.nuance: The crab's flight from the heron into its hole is the husband's flight from the other woman's rage into his wife's house, which the friend reads aloud only by refusing him entry. Lines 16 to 26 are dense and partly uncertain, especially who owes what in line 21.

thinai_evidence.note: a husband's affair and the wife's side refusing him

comparisons.tenor: the wide pond, like the sea
the hollow lotus stalks, like bamboo
the lotus leaves, like elephant ears
the plump buds, like raised stakes
the many flowers, like smiling faces
the crab's eyes, like neem buds
the crab's tracks in the mud, like the streaks of skin spots
her eyes, like flowers

ullurai.tenor: the husband fleeing the other woman's anger back to his wife's house

pairs.situation: he is afraid of the angry other woman who hunts him
he hurries back to shelter in his own house
his flight leaves marks the whole town can read

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a crab and heron of the marutham field pond in a marutham poem (porul 7.27)

177.reading: The friend tells the woman not to despair that her old beauty is gone and he still does not come: though the man who went across the forest (where the sun withers the wazhai on bamboo slopes and a heavy-bellied peahen, craving red paagal fruit, cries like a horn on the Ayiri's bank) has stayed long, he will surely hurry back, remembering the painted designs among the spots on her breasts, budded like the shoots of the tall mango by the shaded pond on the Kaveri's north bank, in the land of Pannan whose spear stopped the hill-like elephants of his foes.
177.nuance: The comfort rests on his desire rather than his word: what will bring him back is the memory of her body, and the land the friend borrows to praise it is a warrior-patron's fertile riverbank.

thinai_evidence.note: he has crossed the forest and delays

comparisons.tenor: her oiled, bound tresses, like a female elephant's trunk
the peahen's cry, like a horn
the enemy elephants, like hills
her breast, like the mango's tender shoots

178.reading: The friend, glad that marriage is settled, tells the woman she joined knowingly with the lord of a good hill where a boar with diamond-sharp tusks drinks from a drum-round spring, gorges on chempu tubers, ambles down a rock shaped like a lying elephant, brushes pollen from the koothalam's flowers and, having grazed the millet, sleeps content: may she live with him for ever, her shoulders unspoiled, for he says nights alone in the cold dew are hard, knows no parting even in dreams, and by his nature loves her more than on the day he first saw her.
178.nuance: The boar that eats from the guarded millet field and then sleeps easy can be read as the man whose secret love is now made safe, but the poem gives no anchor for that, so it is left as scene. The friend quotes the man's own words as the guarantee.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet and the lord of the hills

comparisons.tenor: the boar's tusks, like diamond
its coarse bristles, like bamboo roots
the full spring, like a drum's face
the chempu's broad leaves, like sapphire
the plump tubers, like lumps
the rock, like a lying female elephant
the seeping water, like a river
the white koothalam flowers, like herons perched on a green bush
the fallen pollen, like gold streaked on a touchstone

179.reading: The friend asks the man who has announced his going: if he wants to cross the waste of the sky-touching peak, where the mirage runs, fire has spread, the elephant raises its trunk to the sky and finds no water, the paths are lined with stones carved with archers' stances and no one quells the robbers' uproar, can he bear to live away from home while she of the sweet smile, quill-like teeth, kuvalai eyes and moon-bright brow is left alone?
179.nuance: The road's hero-stones are given as a plain warning of death on the path; the friend sets them beside the woman's face, feature by feature, and leaves the choice as a question.

thinai_evidence.note: the man means to leave home across the waste

comparisons.tenor: her massed sharp teeth, like peacock-quill tips
her kohl eyes, like fresh kuvalai flowers
her bright brow, like the moon

180.reading: It is laughable, friend: while we played at sand houses on the dunes of the grove, one man drove up in his chariot, needlessly hung a bee-thronged wreath of pond kuvalai down her braided back, gazed at her breasts, thought long and left without a word; and for that alone this noisy town now looks at the gold pollen of the bent punnai in the garden and looks at me too.
180.nuance: Under the mockery the friend is reporting a suitor's first approach and testing the girl's response, as the colophon says (குறைநயப்ப); the town's gaze at the pollen and at her is the first stir of gossip.

thinai_evidence.note: the thazhai and punnai of the backwater grove

comparisons.tenor: the punnai's fine pollen, like gold

colophon.thurai: இரந்து பின்னின்றதலைமகற்குக் குறைநேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகளைக்குறைநயப்பக் கூறியது. தலைமகன்சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழிக்குச்சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

links.note: Kural 1157 has the woman say her slipping bangles already announce that the lord of the shore has left; in Akananuru 161 the friend tells the man the girl's tears show she has already understood his plan to go.
links.teaches: The poem turns the couplet's body-as-herald into an argument: the friend uses the tears that announce his going as the reason he should not go, so the sign the Kural records becomes a plea.

links.note: Both are the friend speaking to a man about to leave for the waste; 161 argues from the girl's tears, which already know, 179 from the dangers of the road and the girl's face.
links.teaches: Read together they show two tactics in the same office of dissuasion: one presents the departure as already a wound, the other as a risk set against a beauty left alone.

links.note: In 162 the man tells his heart of the midnight storm and the guarded house he braved to meet her; in 168 the friend tells such a man that the night path, with its tiger and darkness, must be given up.
links.teaches: The danger the lover counts as proof of his love is the very thing the friend uses to end the night meetings and press for marriage, so the same night risk carries opposite verdicts by speaker.

links.note: Both women, left alone, send a non-human messenger to the absent man: in 163 the cold north wind, in 170 the crab of the backwater.
links.teaches: The messenger is drawn from the poem's own season and land, the wind of the rains' end in one and the shore crab in the other, so even the convention of the go-between is fitted to its landscape.

links.note: Both are a man in the king's war camp telling his heart about his wife in the rains; in 164 he waits for the king to release him, in 174 he has turned away from further battle and she does not yet know he is coming.
links.teaches: Together they mark two moments of the same camp poem: the season of return arriving while duty holds him, and the moment he is free but her grief still runs ahead of the news.

links.note: In 166 the other woman mocks the husband's false oath so the wife's people hear; in 176 the wife's friend describes the other woman's public rage and refuses him the door.
links.teaches: Heard from both sides of the quarrel, the affair is fought through what the town hears: each woman's party uses the other's public display as its weapon against the husband.

links.note: In 167 the man, before leaving, pictures the ruined village where he would sleep and gives up the journey; in 169 a man who has already crossed many wastes pictures his wife grieving at evening.
links.teaches: The pair shows the road imagined from both ends of the decision: before setting out it is a desolation that keeps him home, after setting out it is the distance that makes her grief visible to him.

links.note: Akananuru 168 compares the roar of the waterfalls to the kitchen of Udhiyan, bound to the duty of giving; Purananuru 2 praises the Chera king who gave great food without limit to the armies of the war.
links.teaches: The akam poet can borrow the noise of Udhiyan's kitchen as a simile because his feeding was proverbial in puram praise, so a king's fame for food had become a stock measure of uproar.

links.note: In 172 the friend reproaches the hill-man for lovelessness to press him to marry; in 178 marriage is settled and the friend blesses the union, quoting his own words of devotion.
links.teaches: Read in sequence the friend's two speeches show the pressure for marriage and its answer, and her blessing in 178 quotes the very love she doubted in 172.

links.note: Kural 247 states that this world is not for those without wealth; in Akananuru 173 the man says that dharma and helping kin in ruin are not for those who sit at ease, and leaves to earn.
links.teaches: The poem shows the Kural's premise about wealth working inside a marriage: it becomes the husband's reason for leaving and the friend's ground for comfort, and it shows the cost the maxim omits.

links.note: Akananuru 173 places the man's road on the gold-bearing slopes of Nannan of the swift chariot; Purananuru 151 names a patron as kin of Nannan of the golden chariot, whose hill was shut against poets.
links.teaches: Both books know Nannan by his chariot and his hill, but the puram poem remembers his line for a door shut against singers while the akam poem uses his range only for its gold and its danger, so the same name carries blame in one genre and mere geography in the other.

links.note: Both are the friend assuring the woman that the absent man will return; in 173 he will return because of his principle and his promise, in 177 because he will remember her body.
links.teaches: Side by side they show two grounds the friend can give for hope, his word and his desire, so the same office of comfort can rest on duty or on longing.

links.note: Akananuru 175 compares the lightning to the spear Chezhiyan raised after he won the battle at Alangaanam (ஆலங் கானத்து அமர்கடந்து); Purananuru 23 praises Nedunchezhiyan with the same phrase.
links.teaches: The identical phrase shows the victory at Alangaanam was already a formula, so an akam poet could use a celebrated battle to light up a love poem's rain clouds.

links.note: Kural 1154 asks whether those who trusted the assuring word are at fault when the one who said 'do not fear' leaves; in Akananuru 175 the woman recalls his vows, the hand on her wrist and the promised season, which has now come.
links.teaches: The poem supplies the concrete pledge the couplet only names (a vow, a grasped wrist, a named season) and fixes the moment of testing at the arrival of the promised rains.

links.note: Akananuru 177 places a fertile mango grove on the Kaveri's north bank in the land of Pannan of the warrior anklets; Purananuru 173 praises Pannan of Sirukudi as the healer of hunger whose house rings with feeding.
links.teaches: If this is the same Pannan, akam uses the puram patron's land as a byword for fertile beauty, so a patron's renown for feeding becomes a measure of a woman's beauty.

links.note: Kural 1151, which Parimelazhagar gives to the friend, refuses to hear of a quick return; in Akananuru 179 the friend asks the departing man whether he can bear to live away while she is left alone.
links.teaches: The couplet compresses the friend's dissuasion into a threat of death, and the poem shows the fuller form of the same speech, arguing from the dangers of the road and the woman's beauty.

links.note: Akananuru 179 line 1 and Purananuru 151 line 2 are the same line (விண்தோய் சிமைய விறல்வரைக் கவாஅன்); in puram it is the slope of a patron's hill, in akam the slope of the dangerous waste.
links.teaches: The repeated line shows the poets shared formulas across akam and puram, and that the setting decides whether the same sky-touching slope means a patron's wealth or a lover's danger.

new_concepts.gloss: marriage as the end of secret love; the friend's pressing of the lover to marry (வரைவு கடாயது)
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons of 168 and 172 (வரைவு கடாயது) and 178 (வரைவு மலிந்து)

new_concepts.gloss: the appointed meeting place of secret lovers, by day (பகற்குறி) or by night (இரவுக்குறி)

source_issues: 161: line 9 reads தோழ் தாழ்பு, probably for தோள் தாழ்பு (hair falling to the shoulders); the flag also records line 3 as repaired from a joined line.
162: lines 1 and 2 (கொளக்குறை படாஅக் கோடுவளர் குட்டத்து அளப்பு அரிது ஆகிய குவைஇருந் தோன்றல) are obscure in word division and sense.
164: a printed line number 5 stands on line 10 (flag); line 6 ends with a stray closing quotation mark, and line 7 வெறியேன் றன்றே looks mis-divided.
165: the base text has 13 lines, the commentary edition 12 (flag); line 3 ஒய்யென எந்த is unclear (perhaps ஏந்த).
166: the colophon thurai has a stray digit before பரத்தை (கேட்ட 3பரத்தைதன்).
168: the colophon says இரவுக்குறி வந்ததலைமகளை, but the poem addresses the hero (வெற்ப!); தலைமகனை looks intended.
169: line 14 (வருந்துமால், அளியள் திருந்திழை தானே) is repeated as Akananuru 224 line 18 (flag).
175, 180: the colophons give a second speech situation (…உமாம்) without numbering; 175's is split as சொற்றதூ உமாம்.
178: line 19 closes a quotation (…அரிது' எனக்) that never opens.
